title: "peace be with you"
hookLine: "peace be with you" — the handshake in the middle
tomorrow: the obligation nobody explains as a gift

cards: The Mass is quiet and formal. Candles, a priest at the altar, everyone facing forward, nobody talking. And then, out of nowhere, everyone turns around.
The person behind you sticks out a hand. The teenager next to you, who hasn't looked up from the floor, says peace be with you. A couple kisses.
A little kid waves at the whole row. For a few moments, a room full of people who mostly don't know each other shakes hands. Then everyone turns back to the front as if nothing happened.
Today, the handshake in the middle of the Mass.

teach.b: After the story comes the table. Bread and wine are carried up to the altar, the priest prays over them, and the whole room says the Our Father, from day eleven.
Then, just before people come forward for communion, the sign of peace. Where does it come from?

teach.h: PEACE BE TO YOU — EASTER NIGHT.
teach.b: Start with Easter night. In John's Gospel, the frightened friends of Jesus are hiding behind locked doors, and the risen Jesus stands among them. His first words, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Peace be to you."
Not a scolding for running away. Peace. In the Greek of John's Gospel it's eirene, a word that carries the old Hebrew greeting shalom, which means more than quiet.
It means whole, complete, nothing missing. The first Christians greeted each other with more than a handshake: early Christian writers describe a kiss of peace shared in worship.
There's a reason it sits right before communion in the Catholic Mass.

teach.h: MAKE PEACE, THEN COME TO THE ALTAR.
teach.b: Jesus once said that if you're bringing a gift to the altar and remember that someone has something against you, leave the gift there, go and make peace first, then come back.
So before people go up to the table, they turn to whoever's beside them. Not their best friend. Whoever happens to be there.
It's short on purpose. It isn't a chat. It's a sign: before we go any further, we're at peace with each other.
The gesture varies from place to place: a bow, a nod, a handshake. The meaning holds.

how: At Mass, after the Our Father and before communion, the priest invites the people to offer each other a sign of peace, and people turn to those nearby with a handshake, a bow or a nod, saying "peace be with you."

games.q: what's inside the handshake — tap the pairs.
p: the risen Jesus, behind locked doors
make peace first, then come back

s: the sign of peace is a modern addition to the Mass
early Christian writers describe a kiss of peace shared in worship.
in the Catholic Mass, the sign of peace comes just before communion
people make peace with each other before going to the table.
you're supposed to greet only people you know
it's whoever happens to be beside you.

games.q: you're one of Jesus's friends, hiding behind a locked door on Easter night after running away. he's suddenly standing in the room. what's the first thing he says?
games.why: "peace be to you." not a scolding. the greeting Catholics pass to each other at Mass starts here.

practice: Here's the practice. Bring three people to mind, one at a time. Someone you love.
Someone you barely know: a neighbor, a coworker, the person who sold you coffee. Then someone you're not at peace with right now. With each one, picture turning to them and offering your hand.
If you pray, you can wish each of them peace.

wordCard.voice: The sign of peace. Turning to whoever is beside you, just before the table, to say peace be with you. Thirteenth word.

orig.note: Greek: peace. the word John's Gospel puts in the risen Jesus's mouth, carrying the Hebrew shalom behind it.

carryVoice: Your line: turn to the stranger. Not your best friend: whoever happens to be beside you. Day thirteen, done.
